title: Legacy formatting and what a Date holds

questions.stem: Per this page, many threads must format dates through one static field without any locking. Which field is safe to share?

options.text: A static final SimpleDateFormat that has been set to strict, non-lenient mode
options.says: The page says SimpleDateFormat is unsafe because of the Calendar it mutates while working; strict mode changes validation, not that shared state.

options.text: A static final SimpleDateFormat that has been given a fixed UTC time zone
options.says: The page blames the internal Calendar state for the corruption; fixing the time zone leaves that shared state in place.

options.text: A static final DateTimeFormatter built once from the pattern it needs
options.says: The page says DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe, so one static final instance can be shared by all threads.

questions.stem: Per this page, why can the same java.util.Date print as a different day and time on two machines?

options.text: It holds only epoch milliseconds, and toString renders them in the default zone
options.says: The page says the internal value is always UTC milliseconds while toString() uses the default time zone.

options.text: It holds the creating machine's wall-clock fields, and each reader shifts them
options.says: The page says a Date's internal representation is milliseconds since the epoch, not wall-clock fields.

options.text: It holds a rounded clock reading, and each machine rounds it at its own precision
options.says: The page names the default time zone used by toString() as the cause, not any rounding of the stored value.
